learn.hook: India grows more than 50,000 strains of rice and about 1,000 varieties of mango. That variety within just two species is biodiversity too.
points: Biodiversity is the term popularised by the sociobiologist Edward Wilson to describe the combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation. The three most important levels are genetic, species and ecological diversity.

Genetic diversity: a single species can show high diversity at the genetic level over its distributional range. The medicinal plant Rauwolfia vomitoria growing in different Himalayan ranges shows genetic variation in the potency and concentration of the active chemical reserpine. India has more than 50,000 genetically different strains of rice and 1,000 varieties of mango.
Species diversity: diversity at the species level. For example, the Western Ghats have a greater amphibian species diversity than the Eastern Ghats.

Ecological diversity: diversity at the ecosystem level. India, with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries and alpine meadows, has greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway.

example.q: Classify each as genetic, species or ecological diversity: (a) 1,000 mango varieties, (b) more amphibian species in the Western Ghats than the Eastern Ghats, (c) India having deserts, mangroves and alpine meadows.
steps: (a) Variation within one species: genetic diversity.
(b) Number of species compared: species diversity.

learn.reallife: The National Bureau of Plant Genetic Resources in New Delhi stores thousands of rice and other crop varieties to protect India's genetic diversity.

learn.hook: Out of every 10 animal species described on Earth, about 7 are insects.
points: According to the IUCN (2004), the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than 1.5 million. Robert May places the global species diversity at about 7 million.

More than 70 per cent of all recorded species are animals, while plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) make up no more than 22 per cent. Among animals, insects are the most species-rich group, making up more than 70 per cent of the total.
The number of fungi species in the world is more than the combined total of species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.

Prokaryotes are not included in these estimates because conventional taxonomic methods are not suitable for identifying microbial species, and many species are simply not culturable under laboratory conditions.

India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area but 8.1 per cent of global species diversity, making it one of the 12 mega diversity countries. Nearly 45,000 plant species and twice as many animal species have been recorded. If May's estimate holds (only 22 per cent of species recorded), India probably has more than 1,00,000 plant species and 3,00,000 animal species yet to be discovered.

example.q: About how many animal species have been recorded from India, according to NCERT?
steps: Animal species are about twice as many.

learn.reallife: The Zoological Survey of India and Botanical Survey of India describe new species every year, from frogs in the Western Ghats to orchids in the North-East.

learn.hook: Colombia near the equator has nearly 1,400 bird species; Greenland, far north, has just 56.
points: Species diversity generally decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles. With few exceptions, tropics (latitudinal range 23.5° N to 23.5° S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas.

Colombia, near the equator, has nearly 1,400 species of birds; New York at 41° N has 105 and Greenland at 71° N only 56. India, with much land in tropical latitudes, has more than 1,200 bird species. A tropical forest in Ecuador has up to 10 times as many vascular plant species as an equal area of temperate forest in the Midwest of the USA.

The largely tropical Amazonian rain forest has the greatest biodiversity on Earth: more than 40,000 species of plants, 3,000 of fishes, 1,300 of birds, 427 of mammals, 427 of amphibians, 378 of reptiles and more than 1,25,000 invertebrates.

Hypotheses for greater tropical diversity: (a) speciation is a function of time; tropics stayed relatively undisturbed for millions of years (unlike temperate regions with frequent glaciations), giving long evolutionary time; (b) tropical environments are less seasonal, more constant and predictable, promoting niche specialisation; (c) more solar energy in the tropics gives higher productivity, which may indirectly support more diversity.

example.q: How many times more bird species does Colombia have than Greenland, using NCERT's figures?

learn.reallife: India's tropical regions, like the Western Ghats and the North-East, are among its richest biodiversity areas, in line with the latitudinal gradient.

learn.hook: Explore a bigger patch of forest and you find more species, but each extra hectare adds fewer new ones. Humboldt noticed this two centuries ago.
points: The German naturalist and geographer Alexander von Humboldt observed that within a region species richness increases with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit.

For many taxa (angiosperms, birds, bats, freshwater fishes), the relation between species richness and area is a rectangular hyperbola. On a logarithmic scale it is a straight line: log S = log C + Z log A, where S = species richness, A = area, Z = slope of the line (regression coefficient) and C = Y-intercept.
Z values lie in the range 0.1 to 0.2 regardless of taxonomic group or region (plants in Britain, birds in California or molluscs in New York state).

For very large areas like entire continents, the slope is much steeper, with Z values of 0.6 to 1.2. For frugivorous (fruit-eating) birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents, the slope is 1.15.

example.q: For a region, log C = 1.2 and Z = 0.15. Find log S for an area with log A = 4.
steps: log S = log C + Z log A

learn.reallife: Conservation planners use species–area relationships to estimate how many species might be lost when a forest is cleared, as in debates over mining in Indian forests.

topics.title: Why species diversity matters: stability and rivets

learn.hook: Ecologist Paul Ehrlich compared species to rivets in an airplane: pop a few and the plane flies; pop the wrong ones and it falls.
points: Communities with more species generally tend to be more stable. A stable community should not show too much variation in productivity from year to year, should be resistant or resilient to occasional disturbances (natural or man-made), and should resist invasion by alien species.

David Tilman's long-term ecosystem experiments using outdoor plots showed that plots with more species had less year-to-year variation in total biomass. Increased diversity also contributed to higher productivity.
Rich biodiversity is not only essential for ecosystem health but imperative for the very survival of humans on Earth.

Rivet popper hypothesis (Paul Ehrlich, Stanford ecologist): in an airplane (ecosystem), parts are joined by thousands of rivets (species). If passengers pop rivets to take home (species go extinct), flight safety (ecosystem functioning) may not be affected at first, but as more rivets go, the plane becomes dangerously weak.
Which rivet is removed also matters: losing rivets on the wings (key species driving major ecosystem functions) is a far bigger threat than losing a few rivets on seats or windows.

example.q: In the rivet popper analogy, what do the airplane, rivets and wing rivets represent?
steps: Wing rivets: key species that drive major ecosystem functions.
example.answer: Airplane = ecosystem; rivets = species; wing rivets = key species

learn.reallife: Losing pollinators such as bees would hit Indian crops like mustard and fruit orchards hard, a real-world 'wing rivet'.

topics.title: Loss of biodiversity: extinctions and effects

learn.hook: The dodo of Mauritius is gone forever, and so are three subspecies of tiger: Bali, Javan and Caspian.
points: The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species (including 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years. Recent examples: dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia) and three subspecies of tiger (Bali, Javan and Caspian). The last twenty years alone saw the disappearance of 27 species.

Extinctions are not random: some groups like amphibians appear more vulnerable. More than 15,500 species worldwide face extinction. At present 12 per cent of bird species, 23 per cent of mammal species, 32 per cent of amphibian species and 31 per cent of gymnosperm species face the threat of extinction.

Earth has had five episodes of mass extinction. The 'sixth extinction' now in progress differs: current extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times, and humans are primarily responsible. Nearly half of all species on Earth might be wiped out within the next 100 years.

Effects of biodiversity loss in a region: decline in plant production; lowered resistance to environmental perturbations such as drought; increased variability in ecosystem processes such as plant productivity, water use and pest and disease cycles.

example.q: Of the 784 extinctions listed in the IUCN Red List (2004), 338 are vertebrates and 87 are plants. How many are invertebrates?

learn.reallife: The cheetah was declared extinct in India in 1952; its reintroduction at Kuno National Park in 2022 shows how hard it is to undo a loss.

topics.title: Causes of biodiversity loss: the Evil Quartet

learn.hook: Introducing one fish, the Nile perch, into Lake Victoria led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish.
points: The four major causes of accelerated extinction are called the 'Evil Quartet'. (i) Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause. Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 per cent of Earth's land surface but now cover no more than 6 per cent. The Amazon rain forest, called the 'lungs of the planet', is being cleared for soya beans and for grassland to raise beef cattle. Fragmentation especially harms mammals and birds needing large territories and animals with migratory habits; pollution also degrades habitats.

(ii) Over-exploitation: Steller's sea cow and the passenger pigeon became extinct in the last 500 years due to over-exploitation by humans. Many marine fish populations are over-harvested, endangering commercially important species.

(iii) Alien species invasions: the Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria in East Africa led to extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish. Invasive weeds like carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eichhornia) threaten native species. Illegal introduction of the African catfish Clarias gariepinus for aquaculture threatens indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers.

(iv) Co-extinctions: when a species becomes extinct, species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct. When a host fish species becomes extinct, its unique assemblage of parasites meets the same fate. In co-evolved plant–pollinator mutualism, extinction of one invariably leads to extinction of the other.
Exam focus: list the Evil Quartet with an example of each; distinguish in situ and ex situ conservation; explain the rivet popper hypothesis.

example.q: Name the Evil Quartet cause in each case: (a) Nile perch in Lake Victoria, (b) passenger pigeon, (c) clearing Amazon forest for soya beans, (d) parasites dying with their host fish.
example.answer: (a) alien species (b) over-exploitation (c) habitat loss (d) co-extinction

learn.reallife: Lantana and Parthenium have spread widely across Indian forests and farmlands, crowding out native plants, a home-grown example of alien species invasion.

learn.hook: More than a quarter of the medicines sold worldwide come from plants, and thousands of plant species are used in traditional medicine.
points: Narrowly utilitarian reasons: humans get countless direct economic benefits from nature: food (cereals, pulses, fruits), firewood, fibre, construction material, industrial products (tannins, lubricants, dyes, resins, perfumes) and medicinal products. More than 25 per cent of drugs sold worldwide are derived from plants, and 25,000 plant species contribute to traditional medicines of native peoples.
Bioprospecting is exploring molecular, genetic and species-level diversity for products of economic importance. Nations rich in biodiversity can expect to reap enormous benefits.

Broadly utilitarian reasons: biodiversity plays a major role in ecosystem services. The Amazon forest is estimated to produce, through photosynthesis, 20 per cent of the total oxygen in Earth's atmosphere. Pollination by bees, bumblebees, birds and bats gives us fruits and seeds. There are also intangible aesthetic pleasures: walking through thick woods, watching spring flowers in bloom or waking up to a bulbul's song.

Ethical reasons: every species has intrinsic value, even if it has no current economic value to us. We have a moral duty to care for their well-being and pass on our biological legacy in good order to future generations.

example.q: Classify each reason for conservation: (a) neem used for medicines, (b) bees pollinating mango trees, (c) a species has a right to exist.

learn.reallife: India's AYUSH systems use thousands of plant species; protecting forests also protects this pharmacy of the future.

topics.title: In situ conservation: hotspots, protected areas and sacred groves

learn.hook: Some forests in Meghalaya have been protected for centuries not by law but by communities, and they shelter rare plants found almost nowhere else.
points: In situ (on site) conservation protects the whole ecosystem, so biodiversity at all levels is protected: we save the entire forest to save the tiger.

Biodiversity hotspots are regions with very high species richness and a high degree of endemism (species found only there). Initially 25 were identified; nine more were added, making 34. They are also regions of accelerated habitat loss. Three cover India's high-biodiversity regions: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya. All hotspots together cover less than 2 per cent of Earth's land area, but strict protection could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent.

In India, ecologically unique and biodiversity-rich regions are legally protected as biosphere reserves, national parks and sanctuaries. As per NCERT, India has 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks and 448 wildlife sanctuaries. (These are the book's older figures; current official counts are higher, but use NCERT's numbers in board answers.)

Sacred groves are tracts of forest set aside and protected by communities for religious and cultural reasons, with all trees and wildlife venerated. They are found in the Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, the Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, the Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and the Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas (described under Madhya Pradesh in NCERT). In Meghalaya, sacred groves are the last refuges for many rare and threatened plants.

example.q: How many biodiversity hotspots are there in the world, and which three cover India's high-biodiversity regions?
steps: India's three: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya.
example.answer: 34; Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, Himalaya

learn.reallife: Mawphlang sacred forest near Shillong is a well-known sacred grove where community traditions protect ancient trees and rare species.

topics.title: Ex situ conservation and international efforts

learn.hook: Seeds of thousands of crop varieties sit frozen in seed banks, insurance against the day a disease or disaster wipes out a field.
points: Ex situ (off site) conservation: threatened animals and plants are taken out of their natural habitat and placed in special settings for protection and special care, e.g. zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks. Many animals extinct in the wild continue to be maintained in zoos. It is desirable when a species is endangered or threatened and needs urgent measures.

Advanced ex situ methods: gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods by cryopreservation; eggs can be fertilised in vitro; plants can be propagated by tissue culture; seeds of different genetic strains of commercially important plants can be kept for long periods in seed banks.

International efforts: the Earth Summit held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992 called upon all nations to take measures to conserve biodiversity and sustainably use its benefits (Convention on Biological Diversity). At the World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg, South Africa, in 2002, 190 countries pledged to achieve by 2010 a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss.

Related tools: Ramsar sites are wetlands of international importance designated under the Ramsar Convention (signed at Ramsar, Iran, in 1971). The IUCN Red Data Book (Red List) documents the conservation status of species and lists those threatened with extinction.

example.q: Classify as in situ or ex situ: (a) a national park, (b) a seed bank, (c) a sacred grove, (d) cryopreserved gametes, (e) a botanical garden.
steps: In situ protects species in their natural habitat: (a) and (c).
Ex situ protects them outside their habitat: (b), (d) and (e).

learn.reallife: India's ex situ efforts include the gharial breeding programme and vulture conservation breeding centres such as at Pinjore, Haryana.
